response:
Final-generation diagnosis. Two decisive lessons emerged from generation 8. First, **cardinal weighting works**: Weeks-Of-Sales Overhang Weighted By Rollover Risk (fmb -3.62, alpha -3.1%, t=-3.97) delivered the best raw Sharpe (-0.32) and the best coverage (0.138) of any signal in the archive, confirming that the *size* of the overhang in weeks of sales, not merely its rank, is what interacts with rollover risk. Second, **the long side is real**: Releasing Working Capital While Terming Out Debt produced the archive's first fully aligned positive signal (fmb +3.58, alpha +2.0%, t=+2.15, Sharpe +0.27), showing the interaction is continuous rather than a short-tail artefact. The standing tension is that the largest alphas still come from structural quick-asset scarcity (Nothing Convertible, -5.6%/t=-4.74) which carries no slope, while the cardinal overhang carries the slope. This final batch therefore fuses cardinal measurement with the dual lock-up channel (S1), tests the conditioner choice holding the cardinal leg fixed (S2), multiplies the slope-carrying and alpha-carrying legs into one three-way conditional (S3), consolidates the working long side in cardinal form (S4), gives the structural-illiquidity leg a dynamic conditioner that may finally supply it a slope (S5), and settles the window-length/coverage trade-off on the best-Sharpe specification (S6).

---SIGNAL 1---
NAME: Cardinal Dual Overhang At The Maturity Wall
EXPRESSION: MUL(WINSOR(ADD(SUB(RATIO(invt, sale), MA(RATIO(invt, sale), 5)), SUB(RATIO(SUB(SUB(act, che), invt), sale), MA(RATIO(SUB(SUB(act, che), invt), sale), 5))), 1), RANK(RATIO(dlc, lt)))
HYPOTHESIS: Total operating liquidity consumed is the sum of the excess weeks of sales tied up in goods and the excess weeks tied up in customer credit, both measured against the firm's own normal operating level; that combined excess, amplified by the share of debt falling due within the year, is what leaves a firm unable to pay.
EXPECTED_SIGN: negative
REASONING: The two best specifications in the archive each captured one half of this — the dual channel gave the strongest slope (-4.09) in ordinal form, and the cardinal single channel gave the strongest Sharpe and coverage — and because both deviations are expressed in the same units (weeks of sales) they can be added directly rather than rank-averaged, which removes the weighting ambiguity that the critic raised against nested rank composites. This is the most complete statement of the mechanism this search has identified.
INTERACTION_TYPE: composite

---SIGNAL 2---
NAME: Cardinal Overhang Against Quick-Asset Coverage
EXPRESSION: MUL(WINSOR(SUB(RATIO(invt, sale), MA(RATIO(invt, sale), 5)), 1), RANK(RATIO(dlc, WINSOR(SUB(act, invt), 1))))
HYPOTHESIS: The binding constraint is maturing debt measured against the assets that can actually retire it — cash and receivables — so a firm carrying weeks of excess stock whose quick assets fall short of its near-term debt has no repayment route other than refinancing or discounting its inventory.
EXPECTED_SIGN: negative
REASONING: Holding the cardinal investment leg fixed, this isolates the single remaining open design question: whether the conditioner should be a debt share of the liability stack or a coverage ratio against convertible assets, the latter having produced a cleaner alpha (-3.4%/t=-3.35) in ordinal pairings. The quick-asset denominator is winsorized, addressing the instability the critic flagged for inventory-heavy firms without changing the economics.
INTERACTION_TYPE: ratio

---SIGNAL 3---
NAME: Overhang, Maturity Wall And Structural Illiquidity
EXPRESSION: MUL(MUL(WINSOR(SUB(RATIO(invt, sale), MA(RATIO(invt, sale), 5)), 1), RANK(RATIO(dlc, lt))), RANK(NEG(RATIO(SUB(act, invt), at))))
HYPOTHESIS: Three conditions together define the firm that cannot meet its obligations: liquidity recently consumed into excess stock, a large share of debt due within the year, and a balance sheet that structurally holds few quick assets — the first says how the problem arose, the second when it bites, the third that there is no buffer.
EXPECTED_SIGN: negative
REASONING: The cardinal overhang leg carries the archive's strongest cross-sectional slope while the structural quick-asset scarcity leg carries its largest alpha (-5.6%, t=-4.74) but no slope, and multiplying the two bounded conditioner ranks against the cardinal leg is the only construction that can inherit both properties rather than average them. Both conditioners are non-negative ranks, so the sign of the product is set entirely by the signed cardinal deviation, keeping the direction of the sort unambiguous.
INTERACTION_TYPE: conditional

---SIGNAL 4---
NAME: Cardinal Destocking While Terming Out Debt
EXPRESSION: MUL(NEG(WINSOR(DELTA(RATIO(invt, sale), 1), 1)), RANK(NEG(DELTA(RATIO(dlc, lt), 1))))
HYPOTHESIS: The resilience case is a firm converting weeks of stock back into cash while creditors simultaneously push its maturities out; the magnitude of the working-capital release matters, since freeing a month of sales is a different event from trimming a day's worth.
EXPECTED_SIGN: positive
REASONING: The ordinal version of this long-side mechanism is the archive's only fully aligned positive signal (fmb +3.58, alpha +2.0%, Sharpe +0.27), and the cardinal transformation is exactly the change that improved the short side's Sharpe and coverage in generation 8, so applying it here is an evidence-driven consolidation rather than a new bet. Expressing destocking in weeks of sales rather than as an inventory growth rate also distances the leg from the published inventory-growth anomaly the critic identified as a confound.
INTERACTION_TYPE: composite

---SIGNAL 5---
NAME: Structural Illiquidity Meets Rising Rollover Pressure
EXPRESSION: MUL(RANK(NEG(RATIO(SUB(act, invt), at))), RANK(DELTA(RATIO(dlc, lt), 1)))
HYPOTHESIS: A structurally illiquid balance sheet is survivable until creditors start shortening the firm's funding; the year in which the short-debt share jumps is the year the firm with no quick assets discovers it cannot roll, and that transition is what the market misprices.
EXPECTED_SIGN: negative
REASONING: Quick-asset scarcity has produced the largest alphas in this archive but never a cross-sectional slope, and the plausible reason is that it is a slow-moving structural characteristic already partly priced; pairing it with the *change* in maturity pressure converts it into an event-timing signal, which is the one specification that could supply the missing slope. It is also the only proposal in this batch whose investment leg is a balance-sheet stock rather than a working-capital flow, keeping the final generation from testing a single idea six times.
INTERACTION_TYPE: conditional

---SIGNAL 6---
NAME: Short-Norm Overhang For Breadth
EXPRESSION: MUL(WINSOR(SUB(RATIO(invt, sale), MA(RATIO(invt, sale), 3)), 1), RANK(RATIO(dlc, lt)))
HYPOTHESIS: A firm's normal inventory position is better defined by the last three years than by five, because business models and product mixes drift; a shorter benchmark measures the excess against the operating reality management actually faces, and it makes the signal available for firms with shorter histories.
EXPECTED_SIGN: negative
REASONING: The five-year cardinal version delivered the archive's best Sharpe and coverage, and the remaining unexploited margin is the benchmark window, which trades off a more relevant norm and roughly two extra years of firm history against a noisier baseline. Because it differs from the accepted specification in exactly one parameter, the comparison cleanly identifies whether the mechanism's strength comes from long-run or recent-norm deviation — the last specification question left open by this search.
INTERACTION_TYPE: composite

---CRITIQUE Cardinal Dual Overhang At The Maturity Wall---
VERDICT: accept
SCORE: 3
RATIONALE: A defensible merge of the archive's two best specifications that genuinely changes the measurement (unit-consistent addition of weeks-of-sales deviations instead of rank-averaging), though it remains an incremental fill-in of a 2x2 design grid and the unweighted sum implicitly lets whichever channel has larger dispersion dominate.

---CRITIQUE Cardinal Overhang Against Quick-Asset Coverage---
VERDICT: flag
SCORE: 2
RATIONALE: Beyond being a single-cell swap on an already-tested pairing, the conditioner RATIO(dlc, act-invt) has a denominator that can be near zero or negative for exactly the inventory-heavy distressed firms the hypothesis targets, and winsorizing that denominator does not prevent the sign flip that sends the most constrained firms to the bottom of the rank rather than the top.

---CRITIQUE Overhang, Maturity Wall And Structural Illiquidity---
VERDICT: flag
SCORE: 3
RATIONALE: This uses the identical three ingredients as the archive's "Consumed And Structural Illiquidity Conjunction" and differs only in aggregator (MUL vs MIN) and cardinal vs ordinal encoding of one leg, so it is unlikely to be informative about anything except the aggregator, and stacking two bounded ranks on a signed cardinal leg mostly shrinks magnitudes rather than adding a distinct economic condition.

---CRITIQUE Cardinal Destocking While Terming Out Debt---
VERDICT: flag
SCORE: 2
RATIONALE: This is the cardinal re-encoding of an already-evaluated archive signal with no change of mechanism or conditioner, and the stated justification that weeks-of-sales destocking "distances" the leg from the published inventory-growth anomaly is wrong — deflating inventory by sales is if anything closer to the standard inventory-growth/inventory-to-sales anomaly construction.

---CRITIQUE Structural Illiquidity Meets Rising Rollover Pressure---
VERDICT: accept
SCORE: 4
RATIONALE: This is the only proposal in the batch with a substantively new pairing (a slow-moving structural stock conditioned on the change in maturity pressure rather than its level), and it is motivated by a coherent diagnosis of why quick-asset scarcity delivered alpha without a Fama-MacBeth slope; the main caveat is that Δ(dlc/lt) is partly mechanical as long-term debt rolls into current, which should be checked as a confound rather than a signal.

---CRITIQUE Short-Norm Overhang For Breadth---
VERDICT: flag
SCORE: 1
RATIONALE: Changing the moving-average window from five years to three is a pure hyperparameter tweak on an already-tested specification, offers no new economic content, and the coverage gain it advertises is precisely the kind of sparse-history-driven "improvement" the objective warns against.

---SIGNAL 1---
NAME: Cardinal Overhang Against Uncovered Maturities
EXPRESSION: MUL(WINSOR(SUB(RATIO(invt, sale), MA(RATIO(invt, sale), 5)), 1), RANK(RATIO(dlc, ADD(dlc, che))))
HYPOTHESIS: The relevant fragility is the fraction of near-term claims that cash cannot cover: a firm holding cash equal to its maturing debt faces no wall at all, while one holding almost none faces the whole of it, and that uncovered fraction is what turns excess inventory into a solvency problem.
EXPECTED_SIGN: negative
INTERACTION_TYPE: ratio
REASONING: Expressing coverage as dlc divided by dlc plus cash bounds the conditioner in the unit interval with a strictly non-negative denominator, which removes the near-zero and sign-flip pathologies the critic identified in the quick-asset denominator and guarantees the most constrained firms sit at the top of the rank rather than the bottom. It is also economically distinct from both archived conditioners: dlc/lt measures the composition of claims, while this measures the share of imminent claims with no cash behind them.

---SIGNAL 2---
NAME: Cardinal Overhang Against Timing And Cover
EXPRESSION: MUL(WINSOR(SUB(RATIO(invt, sale), MA(RATIO(invt, sale), 5)), 1), RANK(SUMRANK(RATIO(dlc, lt), NEG(RATIO(ib, lt)))))
HYPOTHESIS: Two independent things must be true for an inventory overhang to become a solvency event: the debt must fall due soon, and the firm's earnings must be too small to service the liability stock; timing without a cash-flow problem is refinanceable, and weak earnings without near-term maturities buys years of time.
EXPECTED_SIGN: negative
INTERACTION_TYPE: composite
REASONING: The three-way stack was redundant with an archived conjunction, so instead this replaces the structural-illiquidity leg with debt-service capacity — a flow measure of fragility that has never been paired with the overhang mechanism, and which is economically orthogonal to the timing of claims. Combining the two conditioners inside a single bounded rank keeps the signed cardinal leg in control of the sort direction while adding a genuinely new economic condition rather than a second encoding of illiquidity.

---SIGNAL 3---
NAME: Lean Stock With Improving Quick Position
EXPRESSION: MUL(RANK(NEG(TS_RANK(RATIO(invt, sale), 5))), RANK(DELTA(RATIO(SUB(act, invt), lct), 1)))
HYPOTHESIS: Resilience shows as a firm running its stock at the low end of its own history while its cash and receivables strengthen relative to what it owes in the next year; the operating discipline and the improving payment capacity together mark a firm that will not be forced into a distressed adjustment.
EXPECTED_SIGN: positive
INTERACTION_TYPE: composite
REASONING: Rather than re-encoding the archived long-side signal, this changes both legs: the investment leg becomes a within-firm inventory *state* — the specification that beat flows repeatedly in this archive — and the conditioner becomes the improvement in the quick ratio, a payment-capacity trajectory never tested here and distinct from the maturity-mix change used before. Both legs are bounded ranks built from high-coverage annual items, so the long leg is populated by genuinely disciplined firms rather than by low-growth firms loading on CMA.

---SIGNAL 4---
NAME: Peer-Relative Stock Excess At The Maturity Wall
EXPRESSION: MUL(WINSOR(IND_ADJ(RATIO(invt, sale)), 1), RANK(RATIO(dlc, lt)))
HYPOTHESIS: The benchmark that matters competitively is what rivals carry, not what the firm itself used to carry: a firm holding materially more weeks of stock than its industry is losing the demand race, and if its debt is also short-dated it must discount that stock to raise cash.
EXPECTED_SIGN: negative
INTERACTION_TYPE: composite
REASONING: This replaces the hyperparameter tweak with a different economic benchmark — peers rather than own history — which captures competitive mispositioning rather than internal drift and answers a question the archive has never posed for the flagship mechanism. Because industry adjustment requires no time-series history, the coverage gain comes from removing a five-year lookback requirement rather than from admitting sparse-history firms, and the cardinal encoding preserves the magnitude weighting that produced the best Sharpe in generation 8.
